concurrency_primitives: 2 goroutines (one analyzeCSV per file) + sync.WaitGroup + buffered results channel cap 2 with closer goroutine (main.go:242-268); parsing/aggregation inside each goroutine is sequential; comparison on main goroutine
design_patterns: None named/realized; single-file procedural decomposition (analyzeCSV, printTopCounts, printNeighborhoodComparison, printDataAnalysis, printNeighborhoodBarChart)
questions: What types of 311 service requests are reported most often?
Which neighborhoods have the highest number of vacant building notices?
Which neighborhoods have the highest number of 311 service requests?
Which neighborhoods appear in both datasets, and how do their numbers compare?
How many 311 records are missing neighborhood information, and how could that affect the results?
overview: Single-file, procedural Go program: two goroutines each stream one CSV into neighborhood/SRType count maps, then top-10 lists, one ASCII bar chart and a side-by-side comparison table are printed. Readable and race-free, but the print blocks sit inside the results-receive loop (so 311 sections print empty first and the vacant list prints twice), paths are hard-coded, sort code is duplicated, and there are no tests or named patterns.
stakeholder_value: A Housing or DPW analyst could glance at the comparison table (e.g., Carrollton Ridge 744 notices vs 6,540 requests) and the 26.6% missing-neighborhood figure, but there is no rate, ratio, ranking or interpretation built on the join. Four of five questions are single-dataset top-10 counts and no specific office is named.
issues: Output-loop bug (main.go:272-311): 311 sections printed empty on first iteration, vacant list printed twice
Token concurrency: two goroutines, no pool, sequential join/aggregate
Only Q4 is cross-dataset; stakeholders generic; raw counts only
go.mod declares go 1.27.2 (toolchain auto-download, undocumented); Windows .exe bundled
Hard-coded data paths, no tests, duplicated sort logic, README lacks dataset links
rationale: Full marks for a clean build and two large real bundled Open Baltimore datasets processed by a streaming, memory-frugal run. Low marks for token concurrency, a single-file design with a visible print-loop bug, and mostly single-dataset questions without a named stakeholder or analytic join. 63/100 = D.
